test.title: A later start to the school day

paragraphs.text: In 2019 a secondary school in the north of England moved the start of its day from 8.30 to 9.40 for a two-year trial. The head teacher, Joanne Reid, had read research suggesting that teenagers’ body clocks shift during puberty, making it hard for them to fall asleep before 11 pm.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The school kept the length of the day the same, so lessons now finish at 4.30 instead of 3.20. Sports clubs that used to meet after school were moved to the lunch break, which was made twenty minutes longer.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: At the end of the first year, attendance had risen from 91 to 94 per cent, and fewer pupils were late for the first lesson. Exam results in mathematics improved slightly, but results in other subjects stayed almost unchanged, and Reid warned that one year was too short to draw firm conclusions.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Not everyone welcomed the change. Some parents who start work early found it difficult to arrange for their children to get to school, and a nearby primary school, which kept its 8.45 start, reported that older brothers and sisters could no longer walk younger children to the gate.
paragraphs.label: D

items.prompt: The trial was planned to last for two years.
Pupils at the school now spend fewer hours in lessons than before the change.
